newsitem.title: USA: Saudi prince denies claim he threatened Venezuela.
newsitem.headline: Saudi prince denies claim he threatened Venezuela.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman on Thursday denied a report claiming he had warned fellow OPEC member Venezuela that the kingdom might crank up oil production in retaliation for the latter's quota-busting.
"I did not utter any word of threat or warning," the Prince told Reuters from his summer vacation house in Marbella, southern Spain.

The Prince, a nephew of Saudi King Fahd and a deputy oil minister, made the rare attributable comment in response to an article in Thursday's Wall Street Journal which claimed he had made the threat at last June's OPEC ministerial meeting in Vienna.

"Saudi Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman hinted at a private meeting with Mr. (Luis) Giusti (head of Venezuela's state oil company, Petroleos de Venezuela) that Saudi Arabia might raise production itself to drive down prices and punish the Venezuelans," the article claimed.
"This is not how we do business," the Prince said, adding that he and Giusti discussed possible joint investments in various industrial projects, including refineries.
The Prince said the two had agreed to follow up their Vienna talks with an exchange of visits to their respective countries.

Venezuela is widely believed to producing oil at a rate well in excess of three million barrels per day, compared to its official OPEC ceiling of 2.39 million barrels per day, which would make it the biggest quota violator in the cartel.
Saudi Arabia, Iran and some other Gulf states have been castigating Venezuela and other quota-busters for years for their overproduction, to no avail.
But Saudi Arabia has been particularly careful not to indicate that it would increase its production in retaliation after an attempt in the mid-1980s to regain lost market share collapsed oil prices.
